topic: Notes: CRI, CNI, and CSI in Kubernetes
questions: Tell me about CRI, CNI, and CSI in Kubernetes
What does the note CRI, CNI, and CSI in Kubernetes say?
What about cri container runtime interface defines kubelet talks container?
answer: Notes: CRI, CNI, and CSI in Kubernetes. CRI is the Container Runtime Interface it defines how the kubelet talks to a container runtime like containerd or CRI-O to start and stop containers. CNI is the Container Network Interface plugins that wire up pod networking, giving each pod its own IP and connecting them across nodes. CSI is the Container Storage Interface, the equivalent for storage: how volumes get provisioned and attached to pods. All three are plugin interfaces so the core doesn't hardcode any one runtime, network, or storage vendor. On CRI: the kubelet doesn't embed runtime logic anymore.

topic: Notes: CRI, CNI, and CSI in Kubernetes
questions: Tell me about CRI, CNI, and CSI in Kubernetes
What does the note CRI, CNI, and CSI in Kubernetes say?
What about speaks grpc whatever implements cri swap containerd cri?
answer: Notes: CRI, CNI, and CSI in Kubernetes. It speaks gRPC to whatever implements the CRI, which is why you can swap containerd for CRI-O or even a custom runtime without recompiling Kubernetes. The main RPCs are RunPodSandbox, CreateContainer, StartContainer, StopContainer, and RemovePodSandbox plus image pull and status calls. On CNI: each plugin is just an executable the kubelet or a CNI agent calls with a JSON config on stdin describing the pod's network namespace, and the plugin returns the IP and routes it assigned. Common ones are Calico, Cilium, Flannel, and Weave.

topic: Notes: CRI, CNI, and CSI in Kubernetes
questions: Tell me about CRI, CNI, and CSI in Kubernetes
What does the note CRI, CNI, and CSI in Kubernetes say?
What about cilium interesting because build ebpf policy enforcement observability?
answer: Notes: CRI, CNI, and CSI in Kubernetes. Cilium is interesting because it builds on eBPF for policy enforcement and observability on top of plain pod networking. On CSI: before it existed, volume plugins were compiled into Kubernetes itself, which meant every new storage system needed a core change. CSI moved that out a CSI driver registers itself, and the external-provisioner and external-attacher sidecars handle the CreateVolume and ControllerPublishVolume calls against the driver's gRPC endpoint. That split is why you see things like the EBS CSI driver as a separate install.

topic: Notes: Forward proxy vs reverse proxy
questions: Tell me about Forward proxy vs reverse proxy
What does the note Forward proxy vs reverse proxy say?
What about key difference side re protecting forward proxy sits?
answer: Notes: Forward proxy vs reverse proxy. Key difference is which side they’re protecting. Forward Proxy sits in front of clients, it’s used when a group of users, say inside a company network, need to reach the internet, and the proxy forwards their requests out on their behalf. The outside world sees the proxy, not the individual users. Reverse Proxy, on the other hand, sits in front of servers. It protects and manages the server side, hiding the backend infrastructure from the clients making requests. So forward proxy anonymizes and controls outbound traffic for clients, reverse proxy manages and distributes inbound traffic for servers.

It watches for pods that can't be scheduled and launches EC2 instances sized to fit them. When nodes are underused, it removes or replaces them. What it replaced. The older Cluster Autoscaler scales fixed node groups (Auto Scaling Groups) up or down. You decide the instance types ahead of time, and nodes are often oversized. Karpenter skips node groups and calls EC2 directly. For each batch of pending pods it picks the cheapest instance type that fits, often in under a minute. Main concepts:

questions: Tell me about RTO vs RPO
What does the note RTO vs RPO say?
What about rto recovery time objective long service down before?
answer: Notes: RTO vs RPO. RTO (Recovery Time Objective) is how long the service can be down before the business is seriously harmed: the time from failure to restored service. RPO (Recovery Point Objective) is how much data the business can afford to lose, measured in time: how far back your last good copy can be. A 4-hour RTO with a 15-minute RPO means "back up within 4 hours, losing at most the last 15 minutes of writes." How the numbers shape the architecture RPO drives your data strategy. Nightly backups give roughly a 24-hour RPO, asynchronous replication gives seconds to minutes, and synchronous replication gets close to zero.

questions: Tell me about RTO vs RPO
What does the note RTO vs RPO say?
What about near zero option cost every write waits remote?
answer: Notes: RTO vs RPO. The near-zero option has a cost: every write waits on the remote copy, which adds latency, and a replica problem can block writes entirely. RTO drives your standby strategy. Backup-and-restore takes hours, a pilot light takes tens of minutes, warm standby takes minutes, and active-active is near-instant. Cost and operational complexity rise steeply at each step, which is why tiering matters. The link to SLOs is the part interviewers like. A 99.9% monthly availability SLO allows about 43 minutes of downtime. A single incident that uses a 4-hour RTO burns more than five months of error budget.

answer: Notes: SAST and DAST. SAST and DAST are two complementary ways of finding security vulnerabilities in an application. SAST (Static Application Security Testing) scans the source code, bytecode or binaries without running them. It's "white-box" testing: it reads the code the way a reviewer would.

questions: Tell me about SAST and DAST

answer: Notes: SAST and DAST. - Finds: SQL injection patterns, hard-coded secrets, unsafe deserialization, weak crypto calls, missing input validation. It points to the exact file and line. - When it runs: early, on every commit or pull request in CI. - Tools: Veracode Static (which you've used at First Republic), Checkmarx, SonarQube, Semgrep, CodeQL / GitHub Advanced Security, Fortify. - Weaknesses: lots of false positives. It can't see runtime or configuration problems, and it's language-specific.

answer: Notes: SAST and DAST. DAST (Dynamic Application Security Testing) attacks the running application from the outside, like a real attacker would, with no access to the code. It's "black-box" testing.

questions: Tell me about SAST and DAST
What does the note SAST and DAST say?
What about finds cross site scripting xss injection actually work?
answer: Notes: SAST and DAST. - Finds: cross-site scripting (XSS), injection that actually works, auth and session flaws, misconfigured headers, TLS problems, exposed admin endpoints. These are issues that only show up when the app is deployed. - When it runs: later, against a staging or test environment, often as a pipeline stage after deployment. - Tools: OWASP ZAP, Burp Suite, Veracode Dynamic, Invicti, StackHawk. - Weaknesses: it can't tell you which line of code is at fault, it's slower, and it only tests the paths it manages to crawl.

Examples are Gitleaks and GitHub secret scanning. - "Shift left" / DevSecOps: building all of these into CI/CD as quality gates rather than leaving them for a pre-release audit.

questions: Tell me about Strong consistency vs eventual consistency
What does the note Strong consistency vs eventual consistency say?
What about strong consistency means once write completes any later?
answer: Notes: Strong consistency vs eventual consistency. Strong consistency means that once a write completes, any later read will immediately see that value. So, no surprises. Everyone sees the latest write right away. Eventual consistency is looser. If no new writes happen, replicas will eventually converge to the same value, but in the meantime, reads might return older data. So, strong consistency favors correctness and predictability, while eventual consistency favors availability and performance, accepting temporary inconsistency.
